name: Joint Probability Problem
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Math of Needing Everything to Go Right
lesson.summary: When multiple breakthroughs all have to succeed for an outcome to happen, the probability of getting all of them is the product of their individual probabilities, which shrinks fast, a pattern worth understanding with simple illustrative numbers before applying it, cautiously, to quantum computing's seven required breakthroughs.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter established that quantum computing's seven required breakthroughs are not a checklist you clear one item at a time, they are a bundle that has to succeed together. That kind of requirement, where several things must ALL happen for an outcome to occur, follows a specific rule from basic probability, and understanding that rule changes how you should read confident predictions about any technology with multiple dependencies.

Here is the rule, illustrated with simple, made-up numbers chosen purely to demonstrate the pattern. Suppose you have five events that are each independent of one another, meaning the outcome of one tells you nothing about the outcome of the others, and suppose each one individually has a fifty percent chance of succeeding. To find the probability that all five succeed, you multiply the individual probabilities together: 0.5 times 0.5 times 0.5 times 0.5 times 0.5, which equals 0.5 raised to the fifth power, or about 0.03125. That is roughly three percent. Five events that each looked like a coin flip, individually no better or worse than fifty-fifty, combine into an outcome that succeeds only about three times out of a hundred.

To be completely explicit: this five-events-at-fifty-percent example is a toy illustration built to demonstrate how the multiplication rule behaves, nothing more. It is not a claim about quantum computing, and the fifty percent figure was not derived from anything about qubits, coherence, or cryogenics, it was chosen because it makes the arithmetic easy to follow. Now apply the same reasoning pattern, still illustratively, to the seven breakthroughs from the previous chapter. Suppose, again purely for illustration, that you were generous and estimated each of the seven breakthroughs at a seventy percent chance of succeeding within some given timeframe, and suppose for the sake of this specific calculation that they were independent of one another. Multiplying seven instances of 0.7 together gives approximately 0.082, or about eight percent. Seven breakthroughs that each individually sounded fairly likely combine, under the joint requirement that all of them succeed, into an outcome with much lower combined odds.

It is essential to be clear about what this second calculation is and is not. It is not a real estimate of quantum computing's actual odds of success, and it should not be quoted as one. Nobody, including experts actively working in the field, currently has a rigorous, defensible way to assign real numeric probabilities to breakthroughs like "cryogenics will scale to support a thousand times more qubits" or "someone will discover a genuinely new class of useful quantum algorithms." The seventy percent figure above is exactly as made up as the fifty percent figure in the first example. What is real, and worth carrying forward, is the reasoning pattern itself: when a technology's ultimate promise depends on several separate breakthroughs all happening, the combined probability of the whole bundle succeeding is lower, often much lower, than the probability of any single piece succeeding on its own. This is precisely why a person can honestly, individually feel optimistic about each of the seven breakthroughs in this course and still be reasonably skeptical about all seven landing together on any particular timeline. The next chapter complicates this picture further, because the assumption of independence baked into this multiplication is itself questionable.
